Javier was on his lunch break at the Valencia bike shop when the message arrived: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number has won a new car in the European Mobile Draw. Claim within 2 hours. Pay 190 euros release tax.
His heart jumped. A car. He had cycled to work in the rain for three years. He didn't remember entering anything, but maybe his number had simply been picked. That happened, didn't it?
He sent his sister Nadia a photo of the message with three exclamation marks. Then, because the timer said 1 hour 42 minutes, he paid before she answered.
Nadia called eight minutes later. "Javi. Did you enter a draw?"
"No, but..."
"Then how did you win it?"
He opened his mouth. The payment page had already vanished. The number no longer replied. The car had never existed. Only the 190 euros had been real, and it was gone.

qa.q: How long did the message give Javier to claim the prize?
qa.a: The message said to claim within 2 hours.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling when he read about the car?
qa.a: His heart jumped with excitement, picturing an end to three years of cycling to work in the rain.

qa.q: What could Javier have done before paying?
qa.a: He could have paused to ask what he had entered, waited for Nadia's reply, and checked the sender through an official channel, since a real prize never needs a fee first.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel after the call?
qa.a: Nadia probably feels sorry for Javier and a little frustrated that the timer pushed him to pay before she could answer.

grounding: A young man thrilled by a message saying he won a car he never entered pays a release fee under a countdown, and the fee is all that was real.

In the hostel mess, Tarun jumped up so fast his dal spilled. "I've won a phone! Latest model!"
The message said his number had been picked in a national lucky draw. Delivery in two days. Just pay 2,999 in tax first, through the link.
The table cheered. Someone started planning a party. Tarun's thumb was already on the link, his heart racing. He had never owned a new phone in his life.
Bhavna, the mess secretary, looked over his shoulder. "Which draw did you enter?"
"I didn't. They picked my number."
"So a stranger is giving you a phone, but you pay them first?"
The cheering faded. Tarun looked at the screen again: a spelling mistake in congratulations, a sender number with twelve digits.
"The fee is the whole trick," Bhavna said. "Real prizes don't charge you."
Tarun sat down slowly, face hot, and deleted the message.

qa.a: It asked him to pay 2,999 in tax first, through the link.

qa.q: Why was Tarun's thumb already on the link?
qa.a: He was thrilled, his heart racing, because he had never owned a new phone, so the excitement rushed him past thinking.

qa.a: Asking which draw he entered, then pointing out that a stranger giving a prize would not make him pay first, helped Tarun notice the warning signs.

Hi Sachin,
You forwarded me that email about winning a car in the festival mega draw and asked if you should pay the 12,000 for registration and tax. Please don't. Here's what I did when I got almost the same one last month.
First, I asked myself one question: what did I enter? Nothing. Nobody hands a stranger a car.
Second, I didn't use any number or link in the email. I went to the company's official website myself and found their customer care. They said they run no such draw and asked me to forward it to their fraud team.
Third, I reminded myself that a genuine prize doesn't ask you to pay before you get it.
I also reported the email on the cybercrime portal. It took five minutes.
If you've already paid anything, call me tonight. We'll sort it out together, no lectures.
Lalit

Eight years ago, when I was twenty-five and new to this city, a man called saying he was a customs officer. A parcel in my name, full of fake passports. He switched to video. Uniform, office, flag. He said I was under arrest and must stay on the call and tell no one.

I found the customs helpline on the official website. No such case. Then I called my father, and then the cybercrime helpline, and reported the number.

Madhav was on the last metro home, phone at six percent, when the video call came. A man in a courtroom-style office said a warrant had been issued in his name. "Stay on camera. Don't disconnect. Tell anyone and the warrant covers them too."
Madhav's pulse jumped. Then he noticed what they were asking for: secrecy, speed, and soon, surely, money.

At his stop he plugged the phone into a café socket, found his local police station's number on the official website, and called. The duty officer sighed. "No warrants are served on video calls, sir. Report the number."
He called his brother Vaibhav next, then reported the number to the cybercrime helpline. Four percent left. Enough.

subtype: Helping a parent who is targeted [Observer]
passage:
Sunday night
I came home at four and found Papa sitting straight at the dining table, phone propped on the fruit bowl, a man in uniform on the screen. Papa put a finger to his lips. His face was grey.
On a notepad he had written: police case, do not tell family, transfer FD.
I didn't shout. I sat beside him, took his hand, and wrote under his note: Papa, this is a scam. Real police never do this. Let me.
He looked at me for a long moment, then nodded. I ended the call. His hands were shaking. He kept saying, "Forty years with a clean record, and they said I'm a criminal."
I told him he had done nothing wrong, that these people fool doctors and judges too. Then we called the cybercrime helpline together, and the bank. Nothing had gone out.
He fell asleep on the sofa by eight. I keep checking on him.
Kashish

qa.q: Where was Papa's phone propped?
qa.a: Papa's phone was propped on the fruit bowl.

qa.q: What was Papa feeling when he kept repeating his clean record?
qa.a: He felt shocked and ashamed, hurt that anyone could call him a criminal after forty years.

qa.q: Which of Kashish's choices helped most?
qa.a: Staying calm, writing a quiet note instead of shouting, ending the call, and calling the cybercrime helpline and the bank together without blaming Papa.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Papa to read Kashish's note?
qa.a: It likely brought relief along with some embarrassment, giving him permission to break the silence he had been ordered to keep.

grounding: An adult child finds Papa on a long fake-police call, ordered to stay silent and move money, ends it calmly and reports it without blame.

I'm Reena, Zubin's neighbour. I was on the stairs when it happened, so I can only say what I saw.
It was eleven at night after his board exam. Zubin was sitting on the landing with his phone, eyes red from studying. He said, half to himself, "My gaming account gets locked in 30 minutes?" He tapped the link and started typing fast. I heard him mutter his password.
Two minutes later he went pale. An email said his password had been changed.
He didn't say much. He put his head on his knees. I guessed he felt stupid, but I don't know for sure.
I sat down next to him and said, "Anyone falls for that when they're this tired." Then his father came out, looked at the screen, and helped him reset his passwords and report the message. His father only said, "Good that you told us straight away."

I'm Gurpreet. I sit next to Hafsa in the hostel study room, so I saw how it started.
On Tuesday Hafsa got a text: Your scholarship KYC is pending. Update in 2 hrs or payment stops, with a link. She didn't tap it. She frowned, opened the university portal herself, and found nothing pending.
Then she did something I wouldn't have thought of. She took a screenshot, crossed out the link in red, and posted it in our class group: Fake. Don't click. Check the portal directly. She reported the number on the cybercrime portal too, and sent the same screenshot to her family group with a voice note in Urdu for her grandmother.
By evening, three people in our class said they had got it too. I forwarded Hafsa's warning to my Nani. She called me that night. She had received a similar message about her pension and hadn't known what to do.

Thursday, 10:40 pm
Almost did something dumb today.
At six a text said my bank account would be blocked tonight unless I updated my KYC through a link. The sender looked like the bank's name, but one letter was off. My thumb was right over the link.
I made myself do the boring thing: closed the message, opened the bank's own app, logged in normally. No alerts. No pending KYC.
An hour later someone called, very polite, "from the bank", saying an OTP had come to my phone and I should read it out to stop the block. I said, "Banks never ask for OTPs. I'll call the number on my card." He hung up before I finished.
I called the real number and reported both. At dinner I told Leela, and she forwarded my screenshot to her parents.
Note to self: urgency is the hook. Slow is safe.
Saurabh

qa.a: The sender looked like the bank's name, but one letter was off.

qa.a: They get a clear example of the fake message before it reaches them, so they are less likely to be rushed into clicking.

I'm Charu. In Class 9 our group had a rule nobody said out loud: if Abhinav asked, you did it.
One night he messaged the group: "Real friends would send the screenshot. Charu, you have Mehr's chat, right?" Mehr had told me privately that she liked someone. Abhinav wanted proof to post.

The next week was lonely. Two of them stopped saving me a seat. But Mehr never found out how close it came, and that still feels like the right trade.

subtype: Pressure from friends to prove loyalty [Receiver]
passage:
Coach's note, district kabaddi camp, night two. Usha.
Around ten I found Sunaina, fifteen, alone on the hostel steps, hugging her knees. She said the senior girls were in Room 14 with a bottle someone had smuggled in, and had told her, "If you're really one of us, you'll have a sip. Real teammates don't act like babies."
She said she didn't want to, but she was scared they would freeze her out on court. She had already said no twice. Her voice kept breaking.
I told her she had done nothing wrong, and that a team that makes you prove loyalty by breaking rules is not looking after you.
What I did next: walked her to my room so she wasn't alone, then went to Room 14, removed the bottle and spoke to the seniors. Called Sunaina's mother that night. At tomorrow's team meeting: loyalty means having each other's backs, not daring each other.

qa.q: Where did Usha find Sunaina around ten?
qa.a: Usha found Sunaina alone on the hostel steps, hugging her knees.

qa.q: What was Sunaina afraid of?
qa.a: She was afraid the senior girls would freeze her out on court if she kept refusing.

qa.q: What did Usha do after listening to Sunaina?
qa.a: Usha kept Sunaina company, removed the bottle and spoke to the seniors, called her mother that night, and planned a team talk about real loyalty.

qa.q: How might the senior girls see the next team meeting?
qa.a: They might feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but hearing that loyalty means having each other's backs may make them rethink the dare.

grounding: A coach records how senior players told a fifteen-year-old that real teammates would drink with them, and how the coach supported her and acted that night.
